flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about yourself and why early childhood education matters to you.
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q1 Attempt 1]
Okay, so a little bit about me. I have worked with LUSD for 17 years. I've worked with a vast age group. So I've started off in elementary school with the age range of kindergarten to fifth grade. I started initially as a campus aide, and then I grew into wanting to do special education initially. And so I became a special education assistant in about, I want to say like 2014. So with that, I had various roles in there too. I started off working in the elementary with that as well. I started doing an encore class, and then I ended up doing SLD resource. So I've kind of had my hands in like a little bit of everything. I ventured from there, and then I did. I went to middle school, and then I was doing like SLD classes with middle school. And then I switched over to like this school called Carlson Home Hospital School. I don't know if you've heard of it, but it is a school where they work with kids from kinder to 12th grade. So it covers all grade levels. But we worked in the hospital, so I worked at CHLA. Working with terminally ill students. I loved it for the most part because I had connections with all my families, all my students as a para. And just built a lot of connections. It was very different, but it was very like the most joyous experience I've ever had. Because whenever I get to work with a kid, it's a new experience. It's an eye-opener to different backgrounds. To different personalities. To different ways of thinking and stuff like that. Perspectives. And I like to kind of combine my perspective with their perspective and grow off of it. To show them that there's more in the world and what it has to offer. I'm big, real, real big on students growing and able to find a voice, advocate for themselves. Whether it's... You know, the babies or whether it's like the teenagers, I just want them to find their own creativity. Their own way of exploring and being creative and mastering that in their own way.

It's like that with any kid in general, but I feel like because they're more at an early start, you have more ways of like kind of like molding and showing and teaching and, you know, getting them more engaged because they're curious and because they're curious, you know, you're able to say, hey, you know, this is this is this, you know, this is what this do. flow_transcript_slices.question: Tell me about a time a child was having a really hard moment emotionally. What did you notice about what they were feeling, and how did you respond?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q3 Attempt 1]
Oh, okay. So, I kind of had a lot of that throughout my work experience, to be honest. So, it's kind of hard to really just choose one. But I would say I had a nonverbal student. And I think the thing about her was that she had a hard time with people not, you know, being able to understand what she needed or wanted. And I think a lot of people just kind of set it off, like, you know, like, oh, that's just her kind of being her. And it's like, no, you know, yes, she's nonverbal. Yes, she needs help. Yes, she's frustrated. But why is she frustrated? What can we do to understand her better? So, I took the time in the initiative to sit down with her and just, you know, go through the emotion with her. Like, hey, do you need this? Is this what you mean? You know, on a little bit, she was getting a little frustrated. And, you know, she was a self-inflicting person. So, I would kind of cover, because, you know, I have a thing about kids and self-harm. So, I would kind of cover, like, hey, no, no, no, no. It's okay. You know, like, I understand you're frustrated. But, you know, guide me to what you want, you know, or, you know, show me what it is that you want, or whatever the case may be. But no one's ever took that time with her. It's just a matter of, you know, them being kind of short patient. And it's just like, well, I don't know. So, it's like, she's frustrated. They're frustrated. And their frustration clashes with each other, instead of, like, being the one to kind of step back and go, no, like, let me slow down. Let me kind of bring myself down to her level and understand what it is that she's trying to convey. She might get frustrated, which she did. But, I'm like, I'm here for it. Like, I'm going to, look, I'm meeting you halfway. I'm going to get you there. Just take your time. It's okay, you know. But it's for them to know it's okay. You know what I mean? You're not going to have everything at once. Or whatever the case may be. Just, like, I'm not going to have everything at once. I'm human. They're human, too. So, it's about patience. And it's about having the guidance and the will to understand each other. And that's what I took away from that situation. Because, you know, a lot of people, especially on the special spectrum and stuff like that, in special education, a lot of people don't know the unknown. And they're afraid to address it, which I'm not. So, for me, I'll take that opportunity and say, hey, okay, we're going to figure this out. We're going to build it together, figure it out together, understand it together, achieve it together. Because that's how you make it work. But if you're going to just, I don't know, and then you leave it, I mean, then the frustration lies because you haven't taken care of it. Or took the initiative to even try to take care of it.

flow_transcript_slices.question: Can you share something you’ve learned about children or yourself over time that changed how you approach your work?
flow_transcript_slices.candidate_transcript:
[Q9 Attempt 1]
So I feel like about since I've learned that has so over the years, I feel like that when they come in and stuff like that, I always ask the kid, you know, hey, how's it going? You know what I mean? Just how are they doing in general, in general, because a lot of people don't ask that. And when they come in with different moods or, you know, emotional regulations and stuff like that, it helps them when someone asks them questions about like how they're doing personally, because it can sometimes shift the dynamic of like how they respond to you or how they go about their day. Because it's the little things and they know somebody cares. They know somebody is, you know, genuinely listening. Listening to them. It's not just like, oh, hey, you know, why are you acting like that or why are you being like that? Or you're just kind of like already casting them off as a certain type of person. It's like you're genuinely like trying to understand what they're going through or where they're coming from. And then it's like you're that person like, hey, I'm here to help if you need me. You know what I mean? Or if you just need me to be the ear, I'm here for you. I'm here to listen, you know, just to say I need to talk real quick or I need to get this off my chest. Or I just needed that to just say I'm doing OK or I'm not doing OK. So, you know, I know someone cares. So I've learned that that goes a long way.
